t.2.7.1: Now a family maidservant of Kaikeyī, who had lived with her from the time of her birth, happened by chance to climb up to the palace terrace that shone like the moon.
t.2.7.2: From that palace Mantharā gazed down upon the whole of Ayodhyā, its royal highways sprinkled with water and strewn with lotuses and water lilies.
t.2.7.3: She saw the city richly adorned with costly, splendid pennants and banners, sprinkled with sandal-scented water, and thronged with people who had bathed head and all.
t.2.7.5: Why is Rāma's mother distributing wealth to the people? And why is there such excessive joy among the people? Tell me. Or what is the lord of the earth, so greatly delighted, about to have performed?
t.2.7.4: Seeing the nurse standing not far away, Mantharā, filled with the highest joy and intent on her purpose, questioned her.
t.2.7.6: Then the nurse, bursting with joy and filled with the highest delight, told the hunchbacked woman of the great good fortune about to come upon Rāghava.
t.2.7.7: Tomorrow, under the Puṣya constellation, King Daśaratha will consecrate Rāma, the sinless scion of Raghu who has conquered anger, as heir apparent.
t.2.7.8: Hearing the nurse's words, the hunchbacked woman, filled with indignation, quickly came down from the palace that resembled a peak of Kailāsa.
t.2.7.9: Burning with anger, the evil-minded Mantharā approached Kaikeyī as she lay resting and spoke these words.
t.2.7.10: Get up, foolish woman! Why do you lie there? Danger is coming upon you. Swept over by a great surging flood, why do you not realize your own state?
t.2.7.12: Thus addressed with harsh words by the angry hunchbacked woman who saw only evil, Kaikeyī fell into the deepest dejection.
t.2.7.11: In a calamity that merely wears the look of good fortune, you boast of your good fortune; but your good fortune is fleeting, like the current of a river in the hot season.
t.2.7.14: But Mantharā, having heard the sweet-syllabled words of Kaikeyī, spoke a reply, filled with anger, she who was skilled in speech.
t.2.7.13: But Kaikeyī said to the hunchbacked woman: "Mantharā, is something not well? For I see your face downcast, and you deeply distressed."
t.2.7.16: O queen, a very great calamity has arisen, one that will bring about your ruin: King Daśaratha is going to consecrate Rāma as crown prince.
t.2.7.15: Then the hunchbacked woman, who sought her welfare, became still more dejected and spoke, filling her with dismay and setting her against Rāghava.
t.2.7.17: Here I am, sunk in bottomless fear, filled with grief and sorrow, as though burning in a fire, and I have come here for your good.
t.2.7.19: Born into a family of kings, you are the chief queen of the lord of the earth; how is it, O queen, that you do not understand the harshness of the ways of kings?
t.2.7.18: O Kaikeyī, through your sorrow great sorrow would befall me, and in your prosperity my prosperity too would lie; of this there is no doubt.
t.2.7.20: Your husband speaks of righteousness yet is deceitful; he speaks gently yet is cruel. Because your heart is pure you do not see it, and so you have been thoroughly deceived by him.
t.2.7.21: Plying you with ready but empty words of comfort, your husband will this very day bestow real gain upon Kausalyā.
t.2.7.22: Having sent Bharata away to your kinsmen, that wicked-hearted one will install Rāma at daybreak in a kingdom whose thorns have been crushed.
t.2.7.24: Just as a snake or an enemy, if ignored, would deal with one, so today have you, together with your son, been dealt with by King Daśaratha.
t.2.7.23: In your naivety you have held an enemy, who goes by the name of husband, in your lap like a venomous serpent, cherishing him as a mother would, out of desire for his welfare.
t.2.7.26: So, Kaikeyī, quickly do what the moment demands and what is for your own good; save your son, yourself, and me as well, O you of wondrous beauty.
t.2.7.25: By that wicked man with his false, soothing words, who is setting Rāma on the throne, you, so naive and ever accustomed to comfort, are surely ruined along with all your kin.
t.2.7.28: Having given that ornament to the hunchbacked woman, Kaikeyī, the finest of women, delighted, spoke these words once more to Mantharā.
t.2.7.27: Having heard Mantharā's words, the fair-faced lady, rising from her couch, thus gave a beautiful ornament to that hunchbacked woman.
t.2.7.30: Between Rāma and Bharata I perceive no difference. Therefore I am delighted that the king will consecrate Rāma in the kingship.
t.2.7.29: What you tell me, Mantharā, is most delightful news. What more can I do for you, who have brought me these tidings so dear to me?
t.2.7.31: O you who deserve kindness, there is nothing further, no word more pleasing or excellent, that you could speak to me again beyond this. Since you have spoken thus, I therefore grant you a supreme boon, dearer still; choose it.
